uncited: *   **Input:** A 3D volume dataset, camera parameters (view direction, projection matrix), number of processors $P$, and the set of ray casting optimizations (early ray termination, adaptive depth sampling, adaptive image sampling).
*   **Volume Data:** Regular 3D grid of voxels.
*   **Boundary Cell List:** List of voxels on the surface of the volume (front and back faces relative to view).
*   **Projection Buffers ($Z_n, Z_r$):** Two arrays of size $W \times H$ (image width and height).
**Preprocessing (Boundary Detection):** Identify all boundary cells in the volume.
A boundary cell is a voxel that has at least one neighbor outside the volume or with different opacity properties, effectively defining the visible surface from the current view.
*   Divide the volume into $P$ subsets such that each subset contains an approximately equal number of boundary cells.
*   Each processor $p$ independently scans its assigned volume subset.
*   For each boundary cell detected in its subset, the processor projects the cell onto the image plane to determine the pixel coordinates $(u, v)$ and the depth $z$.
*   Divide the image plane into $P$ large blocks of consecutive scanlines, one block per processor.
*   Each processor $p$ is assigned a range of scanlines $[u_{start}, u_{end}]$.
*   Check if the pixel is "viable" (i.e., $Z_n[u, v] < \infty$ and $Z_r[u, v] > -\infty$).
*   Cast a ray from the camera through $(u, v)$.
*   Perform ray integration (marching) only within the bounded interval $[Z_n[u, v], Z_r[u, v]]$.
*   Apply ray-dependent optimizations (adaptive image sampling) with care to avoid replicated casting at shared pixels.
Typical values depend on hardware (e.g., SGI Power Challenge had multiple CPUs).
*   **Replicated Ray Casting:** Ray-dependent optimizations like adaptive image sampling can cause replicated work if pixels shared by different processor blocks are evaluated independently.
*   **Precision:** Depth values in $Z_n$ and $Z_r$ must be precise enough to avoid gaps or overlaps in the integration intervals.
*   **Time Complexity:** The projection phase is $O(N_b)$ where $N_b$ is the number of boundary cells, distributed over $P$ processors.
The traversal phase is $O(N_r)$ where $N_r$ is the number of viable pixels, distributed over $P$ processors.
Overall, it is linear in the size of the volume and image, with a constant factor reduced by parallelism.
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(V + I)$ where $V$ is the volume size and $I$ is the image size.
The projection buffers require $O(I)$ space.
It achieves good load balancing by combining the strengths of both partitioning strategies.
Leverages optimizations from the serial algorithm.
No extra synchronization overhead for adaptive image sampling.

The static nature of the partitioning may lead to load imbalance if the distribution of boundary cells or viable pixels is highly skewed, though the equal boundary cell division mitigates this for the projection phase.
